overview:
San Marino is a tiny country entirely surrounded by Italy, tucked into the hills about 10 kilometers inland from the Adriatic coast at Rimini. Its 61 square kilometers would fit inside many single cities, yet it is a fully independent state with its own government, stamps, and license plates, and it claims to be the oldest surviving republic in the world, founded by tradition in the year 301.

About 34,000 people live here and speak Italian. The capital, the City of San Marino, clings to the slopes of Monte Titano beneath three stone towers that appear on the flag and the coat of arms. San Marino is a republic led by two captains regent who hold office together for six months at a time, a system in place for more than 700 years.

Tourism, banking, ceramics, and collectible coins and stamps support the economy. San Marino uses the euro but is not a member of the European Union.
landAndNature: The whole country tilts across the eastern flank of the Apennine foothills, climbing from farmland at about 55 meters to the limestone crest of Monte Titano at 739 meters. From the top on a clear day the Adriatic Sea glitters to the east and Italian mountains stand to the west. The climate is Mediterranean, with warm, dry summers and mild, damp winters, and snow occasionally dusts the towers. There are no lakes and no large rivers, only small streams such as the Ausa and the Marano cutting shallow valleys. Vineyards, olive groves, and woods of oak and chestnut cover the slopes, where foxes, badgers, and hovering kestrels are common.
peopleAndCulture: Daily life closely resembles life in the Italian region of Emilia-Romagna that surrounds the country. Kitchens turn out handmade pasta such as tagliatelle and passatelli, piadina flatbread folded around cheese and ham, and torta tre monti, a layered wafer cake named for the three peaks. Catholicism is the main faith, and September 3, the feast of Saint Marinus, brings crossbow contests, medieval costumes, and flag-throwing displays. San Marino enters its own national teams in international sport; its soccer players are mostly part-timers with day jobs, so a single goal becomes national news. Motorcycle racing is followed closely, and Alessandra Perilli won the country's first Olympic medals in shooting in 2021.
history: By tradition a stonecutter named Marinus, fleeing persecution, climbed Monte Titano in the year 301 and founded a Christian community there. Mountains and stubbornness kept the little settlement free while popes, emperors, and Italian city-states fought over the land all around it. A written constitution from 1600 is still partly in force, among the oldest anywhere. San Marino sheltered Giuseppe Garibaldi in 1849 during Italy's wars of unification, and the new Italian state later agreed to respect its independence. It stayed neutral in both world wars, taking in more than 100,000 refugees during the second, though it was bombed in 1944. San Marino joined the United Nations in 1992.
funFacts: San Marino elects two heads of state at once, and they serve together for only six months before handing over.
Three medieval towers stand along the ridge of Monte Titano, linked by a cliffside path called the Witches' Passage.
San Marino's soccer team, made up largely of part-time players, won its first competitive match in 2024 after decades of defeats.
The country has no airport and no railway, though an electric train climbed up from Rimini until 1944.
Collectible stamps and coins, printed and minted for collectors abroad, have been a source of national income for generations.
